newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Burma hits back critics on drugs, human rights.
newsitem.headline: Burma hits back critics on drugs, human rights.

text.p: Burmese Foreign Minister Ohn Gyaw on Tuesday hit back at media and Western criticism that Rangoon was not doing enough to promote human rights and curb drug trafficking in the country.

"The press has been writing wrong reports based on the context of people opposed to the government," Ohn Gyaw said at a news conference winding up the week-long Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) meetings in Malaysia's capital city.

"Myanmar (Burma) has been co-operating with the human rights commission in Geneva and the U.N.," Ohn Gyaw said. "As a representative of the country, what I am providing is what is going on in the country...what I am providing is the facts."
The Burmese minister said a 15-chapter constitution was being drafted by Rangoon's military government after consultation with "all parties".

The slow pace of constitutional reform has been criticised by some ASEAN dialogue partners from the West, including Australia. Burma is a newly-minted member of ASEAN after being formally inducted last week along with Laos.

He did not say if those consulted included the opposition, led by the leader of the Burmese democracy movement Aung San Suu Kyi, who has been shut out from government despite winning national elections.
Ohn Gyaw said the constitution was being finalised "and we're now dealing with a very delicate chapter on power sharing".

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, at talks on Monday among key Asian and Western powers at the ASEAN meeting, said Washington was becoming increasingly concerned that drug traffickers in Burma were laundering their profits through banks and companies with "official encouragement".
"Drug money has become so pervasive in Burma that it taints legitimate investment and threatens the region as a whole," Albright said at the ASEAN post-ministerial meeting.
"This is a challenge we must face together -- and another reminder that it will be hard to do normal business in Burma until a climate of law is restored to that country," she said.

Albright pointed out that Thailand's strategy of crop eradication and interdiction had, for instance, dramatically cut heroin production and increased the prosecution of drug traffickers at home and abroad.
Stuart Eizenstat, U.S. Under-Secretary of State for Economic, Business and Agricultural Affairs, echoed Albright's comments at Tuesday's news conference.
"Our view is that drug traffickers have been investors in the (Burmese) economy and money is being laundered with such impunity," he said.

Ohn Gyaw, replying to Albright's statement, said the drug problem in Burma was a legacy left behind by the country's colonialists, and the military government has been fighting the scourge since the country gained independence.
He said Burma has signed pacts with China, Thailand, India, Bangladesh, Laos and Vietnam to battle drug traffickers.

"The main focus of these agreements is on reducing drug trafficking and production: eliminating poppy cultivation through economic and social development programmes; and reducing the demand for, and consumption of, drugs," he said.

Ohn Gyaw said Burma has also cooperated with every U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency inspection since 1993 and has even produced a manual, "Control of Money Laundering in Myanmar", to prove its commitment against money laundering.
ASEAN's other members are Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, Singapore, the Philippines and Brunei.
